stories.title: Palestine through the ages: a short tour
stories.intro: Ten stops from the earliest written mention of the name Peleset to a 2024 court opinion. Each caption restates what the event card says; open a card for its sources and the points where accounts differ.

steps.caption: Egyptian texts at Medinet Habu name the Peleset among those Ramesses III fought, about 1181-1175 BCE. Masalha treats this as the earliest source for the name from which Palestine derives.
In 332 BCE Alexander the Great besieged and captured Gaza, held for the Persian Empire. Taking the city secured his route along the coast to Egypt.
The Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik built the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. An inscription gives AH 72 (691-692 CE), generally taken as its completion date.
Salah al-Din's victory at Hittin in 1187 opened the Ayyubid period. In the same year Ayyubid forces took Acre, Jerusalem and many other towns.
Daher al-Umar built a largely self-governing domain centred on Acre. An Ottoman naval siege ended his rule in 1775.
In January 1911 Issa and Yusuf El-Issa founded Falastin in Jaffa. It became one of the most influential Arabic papers in Palestine.
On 2 November 1917 Arthur Balfour wrote to Lord Rothschild that the British government favoured a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, with a safeguard for existing communities.
Palestinians call the expulsion and flight of 1947-1948 the Nakba, Arabic for catastrophe. Accounts of why people left differ; the event card sets them out with sources.
In September 1993 Israel and the PLO signed the Declaration of Principles in Washington. It provided for an interim Palestinian authority and deferred Jerusalem, refugees, settlements and borders.
On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice gave an advisory opinion on Israel's presence in the occupied Palestinian territory. Advisory opinions are not binding.

stories.title: Intro to Palestine: the story in order
stories.intro: Thirty-two stops from the earliest name for the land to the courts today, following the order of the five-part "Intro to Palestine" series by the writer Handala (a Palestinian-perspective explainer, so read it as one view) and Nur Masalha's history of Palestine. Each caption restates its event card; open a card for sources, including accounts that differ.

steps.caption: Part 1, the name. Egyptian texts at Medinet Habu name the Peleset among Ramesses III's opponents, about 1181-1175 BCE. Masalha treats this as the earliest source for the name from which "Palestine" derives.

In the early Islamic province of Filastin, Suleiman ibn Abd al-Malik founded al-Ramla as its administrative capital, about 705-715. Masalha says it became the country's largest city for centuries, with Jerusalem as its religious centre.
Ottoman forces beat the Mamluks in 1516-1517 and took Palestine, organised into the districts of Gaza, Jerusalem, Nablus, Lajjun and Safad. Ottoman rule lasted about four hundred years.
Daher al-Umar, a Galilean tax farmer, built a largely self-governing domain around Acre, tied to the cotton trade. An Ottoman naval siege ended his rule in August 1775.
Jerusalem became a special district answering directly to Istanbul in 1872. By the 1900s it covered Jaffa, Hebron, Gaza and Beersheba; Nablus and Acre lay in the Vilayet of Beirut, created in 1888.

Part 1, Zionism. The first organised wave of Jewish immigrants, many from Eastern Europe, began arriving in 1882. The Ottoman government restricted immigration and land purchase; the card gives the figures and the disagreements.
Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi, a former mayor of Jerusalem, wrote on 1 March 1899 for Herzl. He recognised the Jewish tie to the land but warned of the consequences of Zionism. Herzl replied on 19 March.

The newspaper Falastin was founded in Jaffa in January 1911. It addressed readers as Palestinians and grew increasingly critical of Zionism. Forced out of Jaffa in 1948, it appeared in East Jerusalem until 1967.

Part 2, the Mandate. On 2 November 1917 Arthur Balfour wrote that Britain favoured a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, adding that nothing should harm the rights of existing non-Jewish communities.
At San Remo in April 1920 the Allies assigned the Mandate for Palestine to Britain and agreed to include the Balfour Declaration. The League of Nations text took effect on 29 September 1923.

A June 1922 British statement said a Jewish national home would be founded in Palestine, not make all of it Jewish. The October 1922 census counted 757,182 people: 590,890 Muslims, 83,794 Jews, 73,024 Christians.

Violence over access to the Western Wall spread from Jerusalem from 23 August 1929, reaching Hebron and Safad. Jews and Arabs were killed, many Arabs by police and troops. The Shaw Commission reported in 1930.

A general strike in April 1936 grew into a rural uprising against British rule and Jewish immigration. Britain suppressed it by 1939 with troops, air power, executions and mass arrests. Death estimates vary widely.
The Peel Commission recommended in July 1937 ending the Mandate and dividing Palestine: a Jewish state of about 17 percent, an Arab state joined to Transjordan, and a British-held zone.
The May 1939 White Paper proposed an independent Palestine within ten years and limited Jewish immigration to about 75,000 over five years. The Jewish Agency opposed it strongly.

On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly voted 33 to 13 for partition into Arab and Jewish states with an international Jerusalem. The Jewish Agency accepted; the Arab Higher Committee rejected it. Accounts of the motives differ.

Part 3, the Nakba. In the war that followed, more than 700,000 Palestinian Arabs, about half the Arab population, were expelled or fled. Palestinians call this the Nakba, "catastrophe"; historians differ on causes.
On 9 April 1948 Irgun and Lehi fighters, supported in part by the Haganah, attacked Dayr Yasin near Jerusalem. Estimates of the villagers killed range from about 93 to 140; the card gives the debate.
The Haganah took Arab districts of Haifa on 21-22 April 1948 after British forces withdrew. About 15,000 Arabs fled in those days (Benny Morris). The causes of the flight are disputed.
On 14 May 1948, as the Mandate ended, Jewish leaders in Tel Aviv declared the State of Israel. On 15 May the armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria and Iraq entered Palestine.
In July 1948, during Operation Dani, Israeli forces took Lydda and Ramle, and tens of thousands of residents left or were driven out. Accounts differ on the death toll, on orders, and on causes.
UN General Assembly Resolution 194, 11 December 1948: refugees wishing to return and live at peace should be permitted to, and others compensated. Its interpretation is disputed.

Israel signed armistice agreements with Egypt and Jordan in 1949. They set military demarcation lines, left Egypt in the Gaza area and Jordan in the central highlands, and did not prejudice a final settlement.
The Absentees' Property Law of 14 March 1950 vested the property of defined "absentees" in a Custodian. Estimates of the land and buildings affected vary by source.
The Naksa. Fighting from 5 to 10 June 1967 left Israel in control of the West Bank including East Jerusalem, the Gaza Strip, Sinai and the Golan Heights. The debate over responsibility continues.
Part 4. A Palestinian uprising against the Israeli occupation began in Gaza on 9 December 1987 and spread to the West Bank, with strikes, boycotts and stone-throwing. Its end date is disputed.

Israel and the PLO signed the Declaration of Principles in Washington in 1993: an interim Palestinian authority and a five-year transition, with Jerusalem, refugees, settlements and borders left to later talks.
After Ariel Sharon's visit to the Haram al-Sharif on 28 September 2000, clashes grew into an uprising lasting until about 2005. The card lists casualty counts and the Mitchell Committee's finding.

Part 5. Israel removed about 8,475 settlers from Gaza and withdrew its ground forces in 2005. Israel says this ended its occupation; the UN and others say its control of airspace, waters and crossings kept it in place.
After Hamas won the January 2006 election, fighting with Fatah in June 2007 left Hamas in control of Gaza. Israel and Egypt imposed a blockade, which Israel justifies on security grounds.

On 7 October 2023 Hamas-led fighters attacked southern Israel; Israel reports about 1,200 killed and 251 taken hostage. Israel's offensive in Gaza followed, with large Palestinian losses reported by the UN.

On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice advised that Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory is unlawful and should end as rapidly as possible. Israel rejects the opinion.
